scope: Claim-level evidence for flowering behavior, canopy airflow/pathology, wound recovery, pollen/reproductive biology, antioxidant assays, cold stress, and humidity physiology lessons resolved during the Encyclopedia completion audit.
rules: Mappings remain review-pending and do not authorize publication.
Each source supports only the scoped claim and stated applicability.
Quantitative treatment effects remain bounded to the studied genotype, environment, method, and experimental design.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis includes photoperiod-sensitive and photoperiod-insensitive flowering behavior with genetic control of photoperiod response; this distinction supports caution when discussing reproductive reversion and daylength manipulation.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Dowling et al. 2024, The Plant Journal, DOI 10.1111/tpj.16769.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports the lesson's photoperiod-response distinction and the limitation that revegetation behavior cannot be generalized across all genotypes.
claimEvidence.limitations: Does not directly test the cultivation practice called monster cropping or establish a yield benefit from reproductive reversion.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Within the tested greenhouse cannabis system, enhanced air circulation changed inflorescence microclimate and reduced Botrytis bud-rot incidence, supporting the relevance of within-canopy air movement to disease risk.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Buirs, Lung, and Punja 2025, Canadian Journal of Plant Pathology, DOI 10.1080/07060661.2025.2478250.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports the lesson's emphasis on canopy microclimate, air movement, and disease-risk context.
claimEvidence.limitations: Does not establish a universal airflow velocity, fan layout, or disease-control guarantee across facilities and genotypes.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Photoperiod-insensitive cannabis/hemp material has genetically distinct flowering behavior, so developmental time available for recovery from training should not be assumed equivalent to photoperiod-sensitive material.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Dowling et al. 2024, The Plant Journal, DOI 10.1111/tpj.16769.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports the lesson's biological distinction between photoperiod-sensitive and autoflowering/day-neutral material.
claimEvidence.limitations: Does not test topping, bending, defoliation, or define a universal recovery interval for autoflowering plants.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Plant wound recovery involves coordinated local and systemic regeneration signals and cannot be reduced to a single visible recovery cue such as restored turgor.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Omary, Matosevich, and Efroni 2023, New Phytologist, DOI 10.1111/nph.18487.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports the lesson's separation of immediate water-status recovery, wound repair, and resumed growth.
claimEvidence.limitations: General plant review rather than cannabis-specific training research; no cannabis recovery duration is established.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Windborne cannabis/hemp pollen transport varies with meteorology and spatial context, supporting probabilistic cross-pollination risk assessment rather than one guaranteed isolation radius.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Nimmala, Ross, and Foroutan 2024, Scientific Reports 14:20605, DOI 10.1038/s41598-024-70633-x.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports the lesson's pollen-dispersal and source-pathway-recipient framework.
claimEvidence.limitations: Atmospheric modeling and deposition do not directly quantify successful fertilization probability for every field or facility.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cannabis pollen can germinate and produce pollen tubes on receptive stigmatic tissue, while successful seed formation requires more than visible pollen deposition alone.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Punja and Holmes 2020, Frontiers in Plant Science 11:718, DOI 10.3389/fpls.2020.00718.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports cannabis-specific floral morphology, pollen germination, pollen-tube growth, and later seed-formation context.
claimEvidence.limitations: Does not define a universal stigma-receptivity window or color rule across cultivars.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Controlled cannabis breeding requires explicit pollen collection/handling and containment records because cannabis is wind-pollinated and pollen can be mobile beyond the intended cross.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Wizenberg, Weis, and Campbell 2020 DOI 10.1002/aps3.11389, combined with Nimmala, Ross, and Foroutan 2024 DOI 10.1038/s41598-024-70633-x.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports chain-of-identity, pollen-handling, and containment reasoning for controlled crosses.
claimEvidence.limitations: Controlled handling improves parentage confidence but does not equal DNA-confirmed parentage.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Hemp/cannabis antioxidant-assay outcomes depend on tissue, cultivar/sample set, extraction, and assay method; DPPH, ABTS, FRAP, and related measurements should not be treated as interchangeable biological endpoints.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Jacuńska et al. 2026 DOI 10.3390/app16062957 and Chen et al. 2024 DOI 10.3390/antiox13060749.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports the lesson's method-aware treatment of phenolic and antioxidant measurements.
claimEvidence.limitations: In-vitro extract assays do not establish intact-plant stress tolerance or human clinical efficacy.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: Cold response in hemp varies with cultivar, plant age, acclimation, exposure pattern, and measured endpoint, so one temperature cannot be treated as a universal cannabis injury threshold.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports the lesson's genotype-, age-, and method-bounded interpretation of cold injury.
claimEvidence.limitations: Specific experimental temperatures and responses should not be generalized to all cannabis germplasm or production systems.

claimEvidence.supportedClaim: In the tested CBD-dominant cannabis genotype, very high canopy relative humidity altered development, biomass, flowering timing, and cannabinoid concentration, demonstrating that humidity can materially affect crop physiology under specific conditions.
claimEvidence.sourceLocator: Corredor-Perilla, Kwon, and Park 2025, Frontiers in Plant Science 16:1678142, DOI 10.3389/fpls.2025.1678142.
claimEvidence.applicability: Supports the lesson's humidity/VPD mechanism and the need to interpret RH together with temperature and crop context.
claimEvidence.limitations: The study compares specific treatment ranges in one genotype and does not define universal cannabis RH or VPD targets.
